paragraphs: The paper develops Transductive Local Complexity, or TLC, to study how training performance relates to test performance in transductive learning. Its central question is whether localized complexity tools that give sharp guarantees in inductive learning can provide similarly strong guarantees in the transductive setting. The authors give an affirmative answer through a new analysis.

The foundation is a concentration inequality for the gap between test and training losses when sampling is uniform and without replacement. This sampling structure requires substantial changes to the usual Local Rademacher Complexity argument. The authors combine the inequality with a peeling strategy and a new surrogate variance operator to obtain an excess risk bound consistent with its classical inductive counterpart.

Applied to Transductive Kernel Learning, TLC yields a sharper excess risk bound than the existing state of the art. The work also derives a broader concentration inequality for empirical processes under the same sampling scheme. These are theoretical improvements: they strengthen the tools available for analyzing generalization and motivating transductive algorithms.
icml-2025-a-new-concentration-inequality.tldr: A new concentration inequality enables sharper theoretical guarantees for transductive learning through Transductive Local Complexity.

paragraphs: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models into one model while trying to retain their individual task capabilities. The paper identifies a tension between two approaches: global merging can create interference between parameters, while localized merging can lose the usefulness of task-specific details. CALM addresses this tension by aligning local merging decisions with agreement across tasks.

The method has three parts. Class-balanced entropy minimization sampling uses unlabeled data to support merging decisions. An efficiency-oriented framework chooses a small set of tasks for sequential merging, supporting scalability. Finally, mask optimization aligns localized binary masks with global task consensus, aiming to combine their contributions without conflicts.

The central idea is that a useful local contribution should remain compatible with the combined model's broader task behavior. Experiments report that CALM significantly outperforms existing merging methods, shows robustness, and approaches traditional multi-task learning performance. The findings support consensus-guided local selection as a way to preserve specialized capabilities when assembling a unified model.
icml-2025-calm-consensus-aware-localized.tldr: CALM aligns local model-merging decisions with agreement across tasks to reduce interference and preserve task-specific capabilities.

paragraphs: Domain incremental learning requires a model to learn from changing domains while retaining useful earlier knowledge. Prompt-based methods store domain knowledge in learned prompts and combine those prompts across domains. The paper identifies a problem inside this combination: corresponding prompt components can hold unrelated knowledge, so mixing them introduces interference and harms predictions.

KA-Prompt addresses this problem through two stages. First, a greedy search finds older prompts containing knowledge relevant to the incoming domain. These prompts initialize the new prompts, transferring useful information while establishing component alignment. Second, as training changes the new prompts, the method dynamically identifies relevant old prompts and applies adaptive consistency constraints to preserve that alignment.

The contribution is to treat the internal arrangement of prompt knowledge as something that needs coordination throughout learning. Relevant knowledge must be positioned compatibly for later fusion to work well. Experiments on domain incremental learning benchmarks support the method's effectiveness, with the abstract reporting improvements in both learning and inference capacity.
icml-2025-componential-prompt-knowledge-.tldr: KA-Prompt aligns knowledge components across domain-specific prompts so that combining them causes less interference.

paragraphs: Document-level relation extraction identifies relationships between entities throughout a document. Some relationships are implicit or span multiple sentences, making sentence-local evidence insufficient. The paper argues that approaches based on pretrained language models have difficulty incorporating entity interactions and recovering these less explicit connections, even when they provide rich contextual representations.

DocKS-RAG combines structural and semantic information to address these difficulties. It builds a document-level knowledge graph from the available document data to represent connections between entities and relations. A sentence-level retrieval-augmented generation mechanism then retrieves relevant contextual information using similarities between sentences. Hybrid prompt tuning adapts a large language model to the relation extraction task.

These components give the model complementary evidence: the graph organizes relationships, while retrieval supplies related language context from elsewhere in the document. Experiments on two benchmark datasets report improvements across all evaluated metrics compared with state-of-the-art methods. The stated results support combining document structure, contextual retrieval, and task-specific prompting for more comprehensive relation extraction.
icml-2025-docks-rag-optimizing-document-.tldr: DocKS-RAG combines document knowledge graphs, sentence-level retrieval, and hybrid prompt tuning to improve relation extraction.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the internal computations that support abstract reasoning in large language models. Its motivation is a continuing debate about whether observed reasoning abilities rely on structured mechanisms and how robust those abilities are. The authors identify an emergent architecture that processes abstract relationships through three successive kinds of computation.

In early layers, symbol abstraction heads turn input tokens into abstract variables based on relationships between the tokens. Intermediate symbolic induction heads then perform sequence induction over those variables. Later retrieval heads connect the predicted abstract variable back to its associated value and use that value to predict the next token.

This account links abstraction, reasoning over abstractions, and concrete output within a single neural model. It gives a mechanistic explanation for the abstract reasoning studied, beyond observing successful answers alone. The authors interpret the findings as suggesting that symbolic mechanisms can emerge inside neural networks and support their reasoning. This offers a possible bridge between symbolic and neural approaches without establishing that every form of neural reasoning uses the same architecture.
icml-2025-emergent-symbolic-mechanisms-s.tldr: The authors identify a three-stage symbolic mechanism inside LLMs that abstracts token relationships, reasons over variables, and retrieves output values.

paragraphs: Machine learning explanations are often requested to establish trust, including in situations where the parties involved have conflicting interests. The paper focuses on a practical obstacle: someone providing an explanation may have an incentive to manipulate it. In such settings, producing an explanation alone does not make the explanation operationally trustworthy.

ExpProof explores using zero-knowledge proofs as a cryptographic foundation for explanations of confidential models. The concrete technical work adapts LIME, a widely used explanation algorithm, into versions amenable to these proofs. This connects the explanation procedure with a mechanism intended to support verification while maintaining model confidentiality.

The authors evaluate these LIME variants on neural networks and random forests. The abstract presents the work as a step toward usable explanations in adversarial situations, rather than claiming to settle the broader trust problem. Its contribution is to bring explanation methods and cryptographic verification into the same design, addressing circumstances where the explanation provider's incentives are themselves part of the challenge.
icml-2025-expproof-operationalizing-expl.tldr: ExpProof explores proof-compatible versions of LIME to make explanations more usable when models are confidential and parties have conflicting interests.

paragraphs: Training graph neural networks on large graphs can require substantial computation and memory. One approach saves historical node embeddings and reuses them during training, reducing these costs while retaining model expressiveness. The paper examines the drawback of that reuse: stored features become stale as the model changes, introducing bias into subsequent computation.

The authors analyze this staleness and its connection to weaker performance on large problems. Their resulting training algorithm, REST, reduces feature staleness and can be integrated into existing historical-embedding methods. The abstract describes it as simple to implement and reports improved performance and convergence across different batch sizes, especially when stale features are a dominant problem.

Experiments on large-scale benchmarks report performance improvements of 2.7% on ogbn-papers100M and 3.6% on ogbn-products when enhancing state-of-the-art historical-embedding methods, alongside faster convergence. The findings highlight the importance of keeping reused representations sufficiently current: computational savings from feature reuse are more useful when stale information does not undermine the training process.
icml-2025-haste-makes-waste-a-simple-app.tldr: REST improves large-graph neural network training by reducing the staleness of reused historical embeddings.

paragraphs: High-dimensional data can contain hidden groups whose useful predictive structure differs. Learning a low-dimensional representation can benefit from recognizing those groups, while discovering the groups can benefit from finding their relevant subspaces. The paper brings these two tasks together, extending sufficient dimension reduction from homogeneous regression to heterogeneous data.

The proposed mixture of principal fitted components model, mixPFC, jointly performs clustering, subspace estimation, and variable selection. This means the model identifies subpopulations, learns compact representations, and selects relevant variables within a unified framework. The authors fit it using an expectation-maximization algorithm with a group Lasso penalty and establish a non-asymptotic convergence rate for the algorithm.

Simulation studies report better performance than existing methods across various settings, and applications to real datasets demonstrate practical advantages. The broader significance is the joint treatment of heterogeneity and dimension reduction: information about group structure and predictive subspaces can inform each other during analysis, rather than requiring either one to be fully resolved beforehand.
icml-2025-heterogeneous-sufficient-dimen.tldr: mixPFC jointly discovers hidden groups, estimates predictive subspaces, and selects variables for heterogeneous high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a pretrained reinforcement learning system can adapt to new tasks using a small amount of human preference feedback. The adaptation stage does not depend on reward signals. This makes the central challenge one of translating preference queries into a task-specific policy efficiently, using knowledge acquired during meta-training.

POEM learns two connected components. A task encoder maps tasks into an embedding space designed to preserve preference ordering. A decoder maps those embeddings into policies. When a new task arrives, human preference queries help infer its embedding, and the decoder then produces the corresponding task-specific policy.

The approach concentrates adaptation on identifying the task within a learned representation that connects preferences to behavior. The authors provide a theoretical convergence guarantee for adaptation to the task-specific optimal policy. Experiments also report state-of-the-art performance with substantial gains over baseline methods. Together, these contributions support preference-preserving task representations as a route to few-shot adaptation from human feedback.
icml-2025-meta-reinforcement-learning-wi.tldr: POEM learns preference-preserving task embeddings that enable few-shot policy adaptation from human feedback without reward signals.

paragraphs: Asynchronous federated learning accommodates clients with different system capabilities by allowing asynchronous updates. The paper targets two difficulties in existing methods: assumptions that bound differences between clients' data, and learning rates that require careful tuning using unknown system parameters. Delayed updates also create accumulating staleness that complicates optimization.

The authors first introduce MasFL, which uses momentum to combine historical descent directions across clients and iterations. Their analysis removes the need for data heterogeneity bounds and shows that controlling staleness accumulation yields state-of-the-art convergence rates. The stated guarantees include linear speedup with both the number of participating clients and the number of local updates.

AdaMasFL extends this framework by normalizing gradients during local updates. The authors describe this as removing dependence on problem-specific parameters while retaining theoretical guarantees, producing a tuning-free approach in their framework. Experiments report better runtime efficiency than state-of-the-art asynchronous methods and robustness across learning rate configurations and system conditions, supporting the practical value of the adaptive extension.
icml-2025-momentum-driven-adaptivity-tow.tldr: MasFL and AdaMasFL use momentum and gradient normalization to reduce staleness and tuning requirements in asynchronous federated learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with multiple objectives arranged in a strict priority order. Under this lexicographic structure, the agent optimizes the highest-priority objective before considering lower-priority ones. The analysis assumes linear transition kernels and reward functions, extending theoretical work that has mainly addressed single-objective problems.

The authors introduce an algorithm with provable regret guarantees for each objective. Its bound grows with feature dimension and episode length, and with the square root of the number of episodes. An additional factor is a sum of powers of a parameter describing conflicts between objectives. This makes the role of objective priority and conflict explicit in the guarantee.

The algorithm also applies when the linear model is misspecified. In that setting, the bound gains an additional term proportional to the degree of misspecification and the number of episodes. The contribution is a theoretical account of learning under ordered priorities, including how departures from the modeling assumptions affect the guarantees for individual objectives.
icml-2025-multi-objective-linear-reinfor.tldr: The paper gives per-objective regret guarantees for linear reinforcement learning with hierarchically ordered rewards, including a misspecified setting.

paragraphs: The paper connects poor generalization in AI-generated image detection to an asymmetry in learning. A detector can overfit to a limited set of repetitive fake-image patterns, compressing its feature space into a low-rank representation. The authors argue that this restricted space limits both expressiveness and the ability to generalize.

Their method uses singular value decomposition to split a pretrained vision model's feature space into two orthogonal subspaces. It freezes the principal components and adapts the remaining components to learn fake-image patterns. This preserves pretrained knowledge while explicitly maintaining separation between the preserved and adapted parts, supporting a higher-rank overall feature space.

The authors report that this construction reduces overfitting and improves generalization relative to full-parameter and LoRA-based tuning. They also interpret the method as implicitly learning a hierarchical relationship in which fake images derive from real ones. The abstract presents modeling that relationship as an important belief about better generalization, rather than establishing it as a universally necessary condition.
icml-2025-orthogonal-subspace-decomposit.tldr: Orthogonal feature subspaces preserve pretrained visual knowledge while learning fake-image patterns, improving detector generalization.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an efficient prompt-based defense against adversarial perturbations in images. Its starting point is that existing defenses mix prompt patterns without sufficiently emphasizing patterns tied to object meaning. The authors focus on phase and amplitude spectra because these are closely related to particular semantic patterns and are important for robustness.

Phase and Amplitude-aware Prompting, or PAP, constructs separate phase-level and amplitude-level prompts for each class. During training, it adjusts the weights used for prompting according to the model's robust performance under those prompts. This makes the contribution of each prompt type responsive to how well it helps the model withstand perturbations.

At test time, the model's predicted label determines which prompts are applied to an image. The prompted image then passes through the model to produce the final prediction. Experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a more targeted form of visual prompting that connects class-specific semantic patterns with robustness-based weighting during training.
icml-2025-phase-and-amplitude-aware-prom.tldr: PAP improves adversarial robustness using class-specific phase and amplitude prompts weighted by their robust training performance.

paragraphs: Differentially private in-context learning can use synthetic demonstrations to guide a language model. The paper asks how those generated examples can better preserve the concept conveyed by the original demonstrations. Earlier work found that restricting the generation vocabulary improved accuracy, but the theoretical reason for that improvement remained unexplained.

The authors interpret in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference about a concept underlying the examples. This perspective provides theoretical support for the earlier vocabulary restriction method and motivates Plausible Token Amplification, or PTA. PTA modifies next-token probabilities to emphasize tokens that distinctively represent the ground-truth concept in the original demonstrations.

The intended effect is to make private synthetic examples more informative about the task the language model should infer. The method therefore connects token-level generation choices with the usefulness of the resulting demonstrations. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world text-classification datasets validate PTA's effectiveness, supporting its use to improve accuracy in the studied differentially private in-context learning setting.
icml-2025-plausible-token-amplification-.tldr: PTA adjusts token probabilities so private synthetic demonstrations better communicate the underlying task concept and improve in-context learning accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning from expert state trajectories can help transfer policies between environments with different dynamics. However, imitation can constrain the learned policy's performance, and changed dynamics can make some expert states unreachable. The paper addresses both problems by combining reward maximization with imitation from observation while focusing regularization on shared accessible states.

The framework uses F-distance regularized policy optimization. Its constraints apply to globally accessible states, defined as states with nonzero visitation frequency across every considered dynamics setting. This directs the imitation-related constraint toward states that remain relevant across environments. Different choices of F-distance lead to theoretical analyses and a practical algorithm called Accessible State Oriented Policy Regularization, or ASOR.

ASOR is designed as a module that can be incorporated into reinforcement learning approaches, including offline and off-policy methods. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report significant improvements to state-of-the-art cross-domain policy transfer algorithms. The findings support combining reward-driven learning with accessibility-aware regularization when expert experience comes from different dynamics.
icml-2025-policy-regularization-on-globa.tldr: ASOR improves cross-dynamics policy transfer by combining reward maximization with regularization on states accessible across the considered environments.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several views of the same data. The paper argues that contrastive approaches implicitly assume balanced classes, which creates problems when some groups are much smaller than others. It separates the challenge into recognizing the unequal class distribution and preventing minority examples from receiving weaker representations.

PROTOCOL first maps features from different views into a consensus space. It formulates imbalanced clustering as a partial optimal transport problem, adding progressive mass constraints and a weighted KL divergence for class distributions. These components allow the clustering formulation to account for imbalance. The method then uses transport-enhanced contrastive learning at both feature and class levels.

Logit adjustment and class-sensitive learning rebalance the contrastive process to improve minority representations. The approach therefore connects estimating unequal group structure with changing how representations are learned. Extensive experiments report significant clustering improvements on imbalanced multi-view data, supporting the value of addressing imbalance in both the assignment process and the feature learning objective.
icml-2025-protocol-partial-optimal-trans.tldr: PROTOCOL combines partial optimal transport with rebalanced contrastive learning to improve clustering when multi-view data has unequal class sizes.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from nonrandomized data requires addressing differences between people receiving different treatments. Many methods align treatment subpopulations after splitting the data into groups. The paper points out that this reduces the samples available within each group, making distribution estimation and alignment harder when training data is limited.

The proposed approach compares different probability measures over the same complete set of training samples. Optimal transport theory provides an analysis of confounding bias and outcome estimation error in this formulation. The method learns balanced representations by reducing the discrepancy between the marginal distribution and the distribution conditional on a treatment.

Keeping the full sample set in the alignment formulation avoids the data reduction caused by splitting. The authors state that the resulting representations allow an outcome model trained on one treatment group to generalize to the broader population. Experiments with both binary and continuous treatments demonstrate effectiveness, supporting a common alignment framework for these two treatment settings.
icml-2025-reducing-confounding-bias-with.tldr: The method uses optimal transport to reduce confounding through distribution alignment over all training samples, avoiding treatment-based data splitting.

paragraphs: Language models can fail when interacting with tools by choosing an inappropriate tool or using a tool incorrectly. The paper distinguishes these as tool selection hallucinations and tool usage hallucinations. Both can produce incorrect task execution, consume extra computation, and make tool-based systems less reliable.

To measure these problems, the authors introduce RelyToolBench, with specialized test cases and metrics covering hallucination-aware task success and efficiency. They also propose Relign, a reliability alignment framework that expands the actions available to the model. Alongside tool use, the model can defer action, request clarification, or revise its tool selection as the situation develops.

This broader action space gives the model explicit ways to respond when immediate tool use is inappropriate or uncertain. Extensive experiments report significant reductions in tool hallucinations, improvements in task reliability, and more efficient tool interactions. The contribution combines a clearer evaluation framework with a training approach that makes hesitation and reconsideration part of the model's available behavior.
icml-2025-reducing-tool-hallucination-vi.tldr: Relign reduces tool hallucinations by teaching models to defer, clarify, or reconsider tool choices, evaluated through RelyToolBench.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization studies how a stronger model can learn from a weaker supervisor and potentially exceed that supervisor's performance. This paper investigates how the models' internal representations shape that outcome. It seeks a more precise account of which interactions between weak and strong models help or hinder learning.

The theory uses kernels derived from principal components of the two models' representations. These define a space that broadly captures information the weak model cannot learn but the strong model can. Projecting labels onto this space quantifies the strong model's shortfall from its full potential under weak supervision. The analysis also explains how certain supervision errors can be corrected regardless of overfitting.

A practical consequence is a representation-based metric that predicts performance trends without labels. Experiments support this prediction on molecular tasks with transformers and five language tasks involving 52 LLMs. The work thus connects an explanation of the supervision gap with a way to anticipate weak-to-strong behavior from model representations.
icml-2025-representations-shape-weak-to-.tldr: The paper characterizes weak-to-strong learning through model representations and derives a label-free metric that predicts performance trends.

paragraphs: RWKV offers a recurrent architecture with performance comparable to Transformers, but deploying it on constrained devices remains challenging. The paper finds that post-training quantization methods used for Transformers can substantially degrade RWKV performance. It identifies architectural and weight-distribution properties that make a direct transfer of these methods problematic.

Nonlinear operators prevent parameter fusion in smooth- and rotation-based quantization, adding computational overhead. Meanwhile, the larger quantity of uniformly distributed weights makes cluster-based quantization less accurate. RWKVQuant addresses these issues with a coarse-to-fine proxy that assesses weight uniformity and outliers to choose quantization approaches adaptively, together with a codebook optimization algorithm tailored to element-wise multiplication in RWKV.

The reported experiments quantize RWKV-6-14B to about three bits with less than 1% accuracy loss and a 2.14-fold speedup. This result supports adapting the compression method to the architecture and its weight properties. The contribution is a hybrid quantization framework designed around the specific obstacles that the authors identify in RWKV.
icml-2025-rwkvquant-quantizing-the-rwkv-.tldr: RWKVQuant tailors hybrid quantization to RWKV, achieving about three-bit compression of RWKV-6-14B with under 1% accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks models to generalize from limited examples, but conventional deep networks can be expensive to run. Spiking neural networks offer an event-driven approach with low energy consumption, especially for sparse and dynamic inputs. The paper targets their remaining difficulties with complex spatiotemporal features and accurate comparisons across classes.

FSL-SNN combines a self-feature extractor with a cross-feature contrastive module to improve representations while reducing power consumption. Its training objective brings together temporal efficient training loss and InfoNCE loss. These address the dynamics of spike trains and the discriminative quality of the learned features, connecting temporal processing with the comparisons needed for classification.

Experiments report a significant classification improvement on the neuromorphic N-Omniglot dataset. On the static CUB and miniImageNet datasets, the method achieves performance competitive with artificial neural networks while maintaining low power consumption. The findings support combining temporal optimization and cross-feature comparison to make spiking models more effective for learning from scarce examples.
icml-2025-self-cross-feature-based-spiki.tldr: FSL-SNN combines feature extraction, contrastive comparison, and temporal training to improve few-shot classification with low power consumption.

paragraphs: The paper reframes survival analysis as a density estimation problem. Its algorithm takes the outputs of a density estimation model and post-processes them into survival functions. This creates a route for applying any density estimation model within the proposed framework, broadening the modeling tools available for estimating how survival changes over time.

The framework covers several survival analysis settings, including competing risks with multiple event types. It also handles dependent censoring when prior knowledge describes the relationship between event time and censoring time through a copula. That supplied dependency information is an explicit condition for addressing dependent censoring in this way.

When the dependency information is unavailable, the framework instead estimates upper and lower bounds on survival functions. These bounds represent the associated uncertainty rather than requiring a single fully resolved estimate. The contribution is therefore both a flexible connection to density estimation and a way to distinguish what can be estimated with known dependence from what remains bounded without it.
icml-2025-survival-analysis-via-density-.tldr: The framework converts density estimates into survival functions and provides bounds when censoring dependence is unknown.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can struggle when deployment environments differ from its training data. The resulting unfamiliar state-action pairs can make even conservatively trained policies unreliable. TARL addresses this mismatch by adapting the policy during testing using unsupervised objectives, without requiring environmental rewards.

For discrete actions, TARL minimizes the entropy of predicted action probabilities to reduce uncertainty and avoid out-of-distribution state-action pairs. For continuous actions, it measures and minimizes uncertainty through the normal distribution represented by policy outputs. A KL divergence constraint keeps the adapted policy close to the original policy, addressing overfitting and error accumulation during repeated test-time updates.

To limit adaptation costs, TARL updates only layer normalization parameters. Experiments on Atari benchmarks and D4RL report improvements, including a 13.6% relative increase in episode return over CQL on hopper-expert-v2. The findings support a focused form of reward-free test-time adaptation that combines uncertainty reduction with a constraint on how far policy behavior can change.
icml-2025-test-time-adapted-reinforcemen.tldr: TARL adapts offline reinforcement learning policies at test time by reducing action uncertainty while constraining changes to the original policy.

paragraphs: This study measures inference energy consumption across 1,200 ImageNet classification models. It addresses a gap between the success of deep learning and understanding the energy required to use trained models. The evaluation focuses on the relationship between prediction accuracy and the energy consumed during inference.

The authors find that accuracy gains decline steeply relative to increasing energy use. This means that, in the evaluated models, pursuing additional accuracy can bring progressively smaller benefits for the extra energy consumed. The study also identifies factors contributing to energy consumption and demonstrates methods for improving energy efficiency, connecting measurement with possible improvements.

To make the results useful for model selection, the authors introduce an energy efficiency scoring system and an interactive web application for comparing accuracy and energy consumption. These tools make the tradeoff visible alongside the empirical evaluation. The contribution is a substantial body of measurement and a practical comparison framework intended to support more informed decisions about efficient vision inference.
icml-2025-the-hidden-joules-evaluating-t.tldr: An evaluation of 1,200 vision models reveals diminishing accuracy gains relative to energy use and provides tools for comparing inference efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper adapts SAM 2 to few-shot segmentation, where a few labeled examples guide segmentation of other images. SAM 2's video matching ability appears useful, but there is an important mismatch: video frames contain the same object identity, whereas support and query images in few-shot segmentation contain different object identities. Directly matching support foreground memory to query features is therefore incompatible with that training setup.

A Pseudo Prompt Generator constructs pseudo memory for the query, making the matching step compatible with query features. This generated memory can miss foreground content or include unwanted background. Iterative Memory Refinement adds more query foreground features, while Support-Calibrated Memory Attention suppresses background features using information from the support examples.

Experiments on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i validate the design, with the abstract reporting that one-shot mean intersection-over-union can be 4.2% better than the best baseline. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of both the identity mismatch and the imperfections introduced by constructing query memory.
icml-2025-unlocking-the-power-of-sam-2-f.tldr: The method adapts SAM 2 to few-shot segmentation by generating query memory, refining foreground coverage, and suppressing background contamination.
